items.followUp: Define a free radical and give one example.

rubric.why: A free radical is identified by the presence of an unpaired (odd) electron.
rubric.description: Defines a free radical as having an unpaired electron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a free radical contains an unpaired or odd electron.

rubric.why: A suitable example completes the definition.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example, such as Cl· or CH₃·.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid free-radical example.

modelAnswer: A free radical is an atom or group of atoms containing an unpaired electron.

items.followUp: What is an anion? Give one example.

rubric.why: An ion is defined by its electrical charge.
rubric.description: Defines an ion as an electrically charged atom or group of atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an ion is a charged atom or group of atoms.

rubric.why: A cation is one type of ion.
rubric.description: Names cation as a type of ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming cation or positive ion.

rubric.why: An anion is the other type of ion.
rubric.description: Names anion as a type of ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming anion or negative ion.

modelAnswer: An ion is an electrically charged atom or group of atoms.
The two types of ions are cations (positive ions) and anions (negative ions).

items.followUp: State two properties of a proton.

rubric.why: A neutron has no electrical charge.
rubric.description: States that a neutron is electrically neutral.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that its charge is zero.

rubric.why: A neutron has a mass of approximately one atomic mass unit.
rubric.description: States the approximate mass of a neutron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving a mass of about 1 amu or 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

modelAnswer: A neutron has no electrical charge; it is neutral.
Its mass is approximately 1 amu (1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).

items.followUp: What are isotopes? Explain why isotopes of an element have different mass numbers.

rubric.why: Isotopes of the same element have different neutron counts.
rubric.description: States that isotopes contain different numbers of neutrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the difference in neutron number.

rubric.why: Different neutron counts result in different total nuclear masses.
rubric.description: Connects the neutron difference to different atomic masses.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the different neutron counts cause different masses or mass numbers.

modelAnswer: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Since neutrons contribute to the mass of the atom, the isotopes have different atomic masses.

items.followUp: State the main idea of Dobereiner’s triads and the relationship between the atomic masses in a triad.

rubric.why: A triad consists of a group of three elements.
rubric.description: States that Dobereiner’s triads are groups of three elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the group as containing three elements.

rubric.why: The elements have similar properties, and the middle element’s mass is approximately the average of the other two.
rubric.description: Gives a defining feature of the triad: similar properties or the average-mass relationship.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the elements have similar properties or that the middle element’s atomic mass is approximately the average of the other two.

modelAnswer: Dobereiner’s triads are groups of three elements with similar chemical properties.
In a triad, the atomic mass of the middle element is approximately the average of the atomic masses of the other two elements.

items.followUp: How does shielding by inner-shell electrons affect the removal of a valence electron?

rubric.why: Inner electrons shield the valence electrons from the nucleus and reduce the effective nuclear attraction.
rubric.description: Explains that shielding reduces the nucleus’s attraction for outer electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the reduction in effective nuclear attraction.

rubric.why: With weaker attraction, a valence electron is removed more easily, promoting cation formation.
rubric.description: Links reduced attraction to easier electron removal or cation formation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that shielding makes electron loss or cation formation easier.

modelAnswer: Inner-shell electrons shield the valence electrons from the attraction of the nucleus.
This reduces the effective nuclear attraction, so a valence electron is removed more easily and a cation forms readily.

items.followUp: Name two substances that dissolve in non-polar solvents.

rubric.why: The first valid example shows that the student knows non-polar solvents dissolve non-polar substances.
rubric.description: Names one suitable substance that dissolves in a non-polar solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid example, such as oil, fat, grease, wax or iodine.

rubric.why: A second valid example is required.
rubric.description: Names a second suitable substance that dissolves in a non-polar solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second valid example distinct from the first.

modelAnswer: Fats also dissolve in non-polar solvents.

items.followUp: Define oxidation and reduction, and state how they are related in a redox reaction.

rubric.why: A redox reaction involves both oxidation and reduction.
rubric.description: States that oxidation and reduction occur in a redox reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both processes.

rubric.why: The two processes occur together in the same reaction.
rubric.description: States that oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that both occur at the same time.

modelAnswer: A redox reaction is a chemical reaction in which oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously.
Oxidation and reduction take place together in the same reaction.
